Deliberately NOT derived from isFusable / styled / DECLARED_CHANNELS / CHANNEL_TO_COMPUTED / TOKEN_CHANNELS / carriedParts — every instrument in the pipeline derives its denominator from the same filter that decides carriage, which is why a channel the filter never opened scores 100%. This file is the independent one.

cases.construct: button.root { outline-style: none } :focus-visible { outline: 3px solid rgb(145, 202, 255); outline-offset: 1px } — the ring's declared width EQUALS Chromium's own `outline-width: medium` (3px) at rest, so the width never differs between planes (antd Button/Switch: --ant-line-width-focus is 3px)
cases.why: Found on the real antd Button after the first S1 fixture passed: the rest plane computes outline-width 3px (Chromium's medium; style none, nothing painted) and the focus plane declares 3px, so the delta is style+color+offset and the width is 'not a fact' — carried nowhere. The canvas draws an outside stroke only from the outline-color + outline-width PAIR, so the focus ring vanished with both halves it did carry receipted. The width on a plane whose outline-style or outline-color changed IS the ring's width and must ride the state, UA-default or not (P2 exam S1, third half).

cases.construct: `z-index: 10` on an absolutely positioned listbox that OVERLAPS its trigger - explicit paint order, not document order
cases.why: Separated from the inset case deliberately. That one asks where the popover goes; this one asks what happens when it lands ON something and the author has said, in CSS, which one wins. The canvas HAS a spelling for paint order - a child's index in the layer tree - so this is not a construct with nowhere to go; the question is whether an explicit z-index is read, translated, or dropped. Declared REFUSED rather than CARRIED because no ordering channel is in the carried vocabulary today, and a silent drop here means a popover that renders behind the thing it is supposed to cover.

predictedWall.status: EXISTING ledger receipt name. I WITHDRAW the FC-STACKING-ORDER-UNREAD code I proposed in the sealing commit - it was wrong.
predictedWall.why: AMENDED before any run. In the sealing commit I wrote that I had searched all four spec registers and found no stacking/paint-order code, and proposed a new one. That claim was FALSE and I am recording the miss rather than quietly deleting it. spec/channel-table.json classes `z-index` as LEDGERED - not REFUSED - with the note 'canvas stacking is child order; reversed z ledgered on read (layout-item-reverse-z-index)'. So the construct is both modelled and named, and the honest prediction is that this case PASSES by name. `isolation` is LEDGERED on the same reasoning. What IS a genuine hard wall next door, and is NOT what this case tests, is `order`: REFUSED as `code-only:no-schema-channel`, and lowering rule `schema.order-unregistered-channel` is one of only three `status: wall` rules in the whole register - 'worse than a drop, a channel name no registry knows can make validateContract refuse the whole component.'

cases.why: Highlighted and selected are different states of the same list and a combobox needs both at once, so they are two cases rather than one. This one is carried by a PER-SIDE border, the accent bar every listbox uses for keyboard focus: the four quiet siblings reserve the same 3px so nothing shifts when the highlight moves, which means the construct is entirely a border COLOUR difference on one edge. A per-side border that collapses to a uniform stroke takes the direction of the highlight with it.

predictedWall.status: EXISTING (note the British -ISED spelling). FC-DUMP-PROPOSE-STROKE-WEIGHT-SIDES is the adjacent CLOSED finding and does NOT cover this.
predictedWall.why: AMENDED before any run - upgraded from `hard`. In the sealing commit I leaned on FC-DUMP-PROPOSE-STROKE-WEIGHT-SIDES being closed and flagged, correctly, that it was about stroke WEIGHT per side while this case varies stroke COLOUR per side. The survey settles it against me: spec/channel-table.json's border-{top,right,bottom,left}-color rows all read 'one strokes paint serves all four sides - lowered only when every carried side agrees.' This case's four quiet options carry a TRANSPARENT left border and the highlighted one carries an opaque blue left border, so the sides do NOT agree by construction, and a single strokes paint cannot hold the difference. The nearest precedent for the shape of the refusal is `propose.radii-not-uniform-refused` - 'border-radius is a single channel and four differing bindings are not representable', which drops all four corner bindings with no per-corner fallback. I predict the accent bar comes back on all four sides or not at all.

predictedWall.status: P10 is an EXISTING pattern code in extract/figma/gauntlet/PATTERN-TAXONOMY.md, explicitly marked NOT EXPRESSIBLE. It is not an FC-* code; no FC-* code covers this.
predictedWall.why: AMENDED before any run - upgraded from `hard`. PATTERN-TAXONOMY.md defines P10 as 'Selected-item state inside a collection' and marks it, in terms, NOT EXPRESSIBLE today - while its neighbour P9 'Repeated-children collection' IS inferred, but only on the canvas->contract leg. The DON'T rule D5 in the same file carries the refusal string 'collection with one deviating item - repeated-children pattern, no vocabulary (P9)', which is a description of this case's markup. Separately, spec/channel-table.json's state-plane inventory drives exactly six planes (default, hover, active, focus-visible, disabled, checked); `selected` appears in NEITHER the driven list NOR the FC-STATE-PLANE-UNDRIVEN list, so it falls to the generic door `fuse.state-outside-vocabulary` ('CONTRACT_STATES is the closed state vocabulary' - drops the binding). Note this case expresses selection as a STATIC fill on a sibling rather than as a state plane, which is the friendlier of the two spellings; if even that is folded away, the harder spelling has no chance.

cases.construct: the OPEN listbox as an out-of-flow overlay - `position: absolute; top: 34px` under a `position: relative` trigger, so the popover does not participate in the trigger's flow
cases.why: 'Overlays rather than reflows' is the one structural fact that separates a combobox from an accordion, and it is carried entirely by the popover being out of flow. The `top: 34px` inset is what places it just under the trigger; if the inset is lost the list lands ON the trigger, and if the out-of-flow-ness is lost the trigger grows to contain the list. Both failures are recognisable at a glance and neither is a colour.

predictedWall.status: EXISTING lowering-register ids (lowercase dotted, not FC-*). FC-RT-OUT-OF-FLOW-PLACEMENT-REFUSED is the emit-side code for the same failure.
predictedWall.why: AMENDED before any run - upgraded from `hard`, and this is the single most precisely grounded prediction in the set. spec/lowering.json `emit.position-inset-overlay-four-sides` fires ONLY when ALL FOUR insets are present as px. This case declares TWO (top and left), which lands it in that rule's own stated loss: 'for a part with one to three insets, the overlay lowering entirely, with nothing said', `receipt: {channel: "none"}`. The sibling rule `emit.position-no-inset-falls-in-flow` spells out the consequence: 'the part now occupies space in the auto-layout it should have been lifted out of' - again `receipt: {channel: "none"}`. That is verbatim the combobox failure this case exists to catch: the popover REFLOWS the trigger instead of overlaying it. FC-RT-OUT-OF-FLOW-PLACEMENT-REFUSED (core/emit-figma-script.ts:6536, :6609, :7382) is the loud version of the same outcome - 'the out-of-flow placement was refused (parent not auto-layout); the child stayed in flow'. I predict the QUIET version, because two insets is the un-receipted branch. I chose two insets deliberately: a popover anchored under a trigger is a two-inset shape in every real library, and the four-inset rule does not describe it.

cases.construct: a div-built table whose HEADER row differs from the body rows by weight (700) and fill - no table formatting context involved
cases.why: The one property that makes a table read as a table. Built out of flex rows on purpose, so it measures the header/body DISTINCTION rather than dying on the `display: table` wall the semantic case pins. If this fails, no data table is drawable by any route; if it passes, the div-table is a viable shape and the semantic-markup refusal is a spelling problem rather than an archetype problem.

canvas.note: the header row is a frame with its own fill and a bolder text style

mustHave: the table header row is visually distinct from the body rows
the header row's text is bolder than the body rows' text
the header row has a different background fill from the body rows
the header row sits above both body rows

cases.construct: real <table> markup: thead/tbody row GROUPS, whose UA display is `table-header-group` / `table-row-group` - a formatting context with no box of its own
cases.why: `display: table` on a div is already pinned REFUSED (display-out-of-vocab). This case is the OTHER half of the same archetype and the one every real data table actually ships: the row-group wrappers the UA stylesheet creates, which are neither `table` nor any display value in the carried vocabulary. A data table cannot be proven without knowing what happens to thead/tbody, and the answer must be a NAME, because a row group that is silently flattened takes the header/body distinction with it.

canvas.note: AutoLayout has no table formatting context and no row-group concept

All four strings are visible verbatim in examples/mui/contracts/table.extension.json:4379-4418. So the honest prediction is now that this case PASSES - the groups are lowered to a flex stack and NAMED - and I have withdrawn the proposed code rather than leave a claim of 'no name exists' standing against a name that does. What remains genuinely un-named is narrower and I am not testing it here: `fuse.table-column-arity-disagreement` drops width AND height for EVERY cell of the whole table on any colspan, whose counter-example in the register reads 'Any colspan in the corpus disables column widths table-wide.'

cases.construct: zebra striping by STRUCTURAL SELECTOR - `.cf-a:nth-child(even) { background-color }` over 6 otherwise identical rows
cases.why: Zebra rules are how every data table in every library separates its rows, and they are the one paint in a table that no element ASKS for - it arrives from the element's position among its siblings. A reader that matches rules to elements has to evaluate `:nth-child` to see it at all. This is also the sharpest form of the repetition question: six identical rows where three of them are a different colour for a reason found nowhere in their own markup.

canvas.note: alternating row fills; on the canvas the stripe is a literal fill per row, not a rule

mustHave: the table shows 6 rows
rows alternate between two background fills, starting with the un-tinted one
exactly 3 rows carry the tinted fill (rows 2, 4 and 6)
the stripe is visible as a fill on the row, not as a border or a gap

predictedWall.status: PROPOSED - no existing code covers this
predictedWall.why: AMENDED before any run - upgraded from `hard`. A repo-wide search for nth-child/zebra finds no code, no door and no lowering rule; the only hits are internal showcase CSS and two RESEARCH mentions (docs/research/enterprise-components.md:227 proposes a `tokensWhen` 'nth-child token flip'; PATTERN-TAXONOMY.md:116 lists zebra as a Table variant axis). What DOES exist is generic and subtractive: the selector-grammar doors `libcss.pseudo-attribute-refusal` ('Any other pseudo or attribute selector is not promotable' - drops the rule) and `libcss.combinator-refusal`. A structural pseudo-class like :nth-child(even) falls to those, which means the stripe is dropped by a door whose receipt names the SELECTOR GRAMMAR rather than the stripe. Zebra striping is how every data table in every library separates its rows, and it has no name of its own.

cases.construct: text-indent: 9999px on a box pinned to 8px (the status-pip idiom: the label is pushed out of the box and only the dot shows)
cases.why: The idiom that hides a label without removing it — altitude's Badge dot plane, and the -9999px half of it is the classic visually-hidden rule. `text-indent` is an ANNOTATE channel: Figma text nodes have no first-line indent. Annotating is honest only while the canvas still draws what the browser draws, and here the browser paints NO text in the box, so drawing the label at indent 0 does not lose a fact — it invents one. The first fresh mint of altitude's Badge came back with 'Badge' painted across an 8px pip and over its neighbouring cells. This case pins the measurement (Part.textOutOfBox, fuse.ts textOutOfBoxEvidence) that lets the canvas withhold exactly the ink CSS withholds.
cases.expectWhere: anatomy.root.tokens.text-indent + the text-indent code-only fact (Part.textOutOfBox withholds the label)

canvas.note: Figma text nodes have no first-line indent; the measured off-box evidence draws no text child at all rather than a label at indent 0

cases.why: A disabled input’s grey text: the painted colour is the fill, NOT `color`. Carrying `color` carried a lie — the contract minted #111111 for text the browser drew in #999999, with no receipt anywhere. MANIFEST EDIT (conformance-frontier round, R1): the engine's behaviour genuinely changed. `-webkit-text-fill-color` is now FOLDED INTO `color` at the read boundary (lib.ts foldTextFillColor, applied at both the capture and the replay/regate boundaries), so the case is re-declared CARRIED on the channel that carries it. Declaring it CARRIED on `color` is strictly STRONGER than the old UNSUPPORTED: it asserts the contract equals the PAINTED INK, so reverting the fold turns the case red (the reader would record color: rgb(17,17,17) and the prediction would fail) instead of passing on the mere presence of the string '-webkit-text-fill-color' in some receipt.

canvas.note: the text fill IS the ink the canvas draws — and now it is the ink the contract mints (verified in the subject browser: with the fill set, the rasterised glyph is rgb(153,153,153); the authored `color` rgb(17,17,17) paints nowhere)
